subject: physics
question_text: Discuss the role of surface tension in the removal of dirt from clothes using detergents.

mark_split.label: Water alone does not wet greasy cloth
A detergent molecule has two ends
Grease is lifted off and rinsed away

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 12 (printed p.110). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: water alone has a high surface tension and forms beads on a greasy cloth rather than spreading into the fibres; a detergent molecule has one end attracted to water and one end attracted to grease; adding detergent lowers the surface tension of water, letting it spread into the cloth, and the grease-attracted ends surround each drop of grease and lift it off the fibre, after which it is carried away with the rinse water.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Water alone does not wet greasy cloth
steps.mark_note: High T, water beads on grease
lines: Water on its own has a high surface
tension. On a greasy cloth it forms
small round beads rather than
spreading into the fibres.
So water alone does not clean a
greasy cloth well.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that water's high surface tension makes it bead, not spread, on grease.
steps.why: Cleaning needs water to reach the fibre under the grease, and a high surface tension keeps the water contracted instead of spreading over the grease.
common_mistakes: Saying water cannot wet cloth at all. It wets clean cloth; the problem is the grease.
Leaving out the reason, and stating only that water alone does not clean well.

recall.must_convey: That water alone has a high surface tension and beads on a greasy cloth instead of spreading into the fibres.
accept: does not spread into the fibres
reject: one end attracted to water, one to grease

steps.memory_tip: High tension: water beads, it does not spread.

steps.label: A detergent molecule has two ends
lines: A detergent molecule has two ends of
different character: one end is
attracted to water, and the other
end is attracted to grease.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name both ends: one attracted to water, one to grease.
steps.why: A molecule with only one kind of end could not link the water being rinsed away to the grease being removed.
common_mistakes: Naming only one end of the molecule and leaving out the other.
Saying the whole molecule is attracted to water, with no separate grease-attracted end.

recall.must_convey: That a detergent molecule has one end attracted to water and one end attracted to grease.

steps.memory_tip: Two ends, two attractions: one for water, one for grease.

steps.label: Detergent lowers T, water spreads
steps.mark_note: Lower T, water spreads into cloth
lines: Adding detergent lowers the surface
tension of water, so the water now
spreads into the cloth instead of
beading on it, and reaches the
fibres under the grease.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Say detergent lowers the surface tension, so water spreads into the cloth.
steps.why: A lower surface tension is what turns the beading water of the first step into water that spreads and reaches the grease.
common_mistakes: Saying detergent raises the surface tension of water. It lowers it.
Skipping the spreading step and moving straight to the grease being lifted off.

recall.must_convey: That detergent lowers the surface tension of water, so it spreads into the cloth and reaches the grease.
accept: reaches the fibres under the grease
reject: carried away with the rinse water

steps.memory_tip: Detergent lowers T, so water spreads instead of beading.

steps.label: Grease is lifted off and rinsed away
steps.mark_note: Grease-loving ends lift off the dirt
lines: The grease-attracted ends of the
detergent molecules surround each
drop of grease, and lift it off the
fibre.
The loosened dirt is then carried
away with the rinse water.
Lower T ⇒ spreads ⇒ grease lifted off
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Say the grease-attracted ends surround the grease and lift it off; the dirt leaves with the rinse water.
steps.why: The grease-attracted ends are what physically detach the grease from the fibre, so naming them is what completes the mechanism, not just the spreading.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the water spreading into the cloth, and never saying how the grease is actually removed.
Saying the detergent dissolves the grease. It surrounds and lifts it off; the grease is carried away, not dissolved.

recall.must_convey: That the grease-attracted ends of the detergent surround each grease drop and lift it off the fibre, and it is carried away with the rinse water.
accept: carried away with the rinse water

steps.memory_tip: The grease-attracted ends surround the grease; the rinse carries it away.

insider_note: The third and fourth marks are often merged into one sentence — spreading into the cloth and lifting off the grease are two separate steps, and both must appear.
